data.title: Key turns to acquisitions amid middle-market M&A lull
data.description:
• Key takeaway: After a nine-year hiatus, KeyCorp has announced two capital-markets deals this year. Executives said the company would consider additional transactions. 
  • Supporting data: Atlantic-Pacific Capital, Key's latest acquisition target, has raised about $123 billion of capital across more than 180 deals. 

 

Two recent acquisitions by KeyCorp should offset recent softness in middle-market merger-and-acquisitions, keeping the Cleveland-based company on track to hit the 2028 revenue target for its capital-markets business, a top executive said.

Key announced a deal to acquire New York-based Atlantic-Pacific Capital on Tuesday, just three months after closing its purchase of Clearwater Corporate Finance.

Randy Paine, the head of Key's institutional bank, said at a conference Thursday that he expects Clearwater to contribute $10 million to $15 million in the fourth quarter, following roughly $10 million in the third quarter.

Paine also told American Banker that the deal for Atlantic-Pacific Capital, which Key expects to close early in 2027, "certainly helps us."

The $191 billion-asset bank reported $540 million in capital-markets revenue through the first nine months of 2026. The contribution from Clearwater, a London-based investment advisory firm, came between the deal's closing in early August and the end of September. 

While Key bought Clearwater to expand its global reach, its deal for Atlantic-Pacific adds private capital advisory capabilities. It also brings expertise in how to create continuation vehicles, a liquidity instrument that private equity firms are increasingly relying on to retain control of high-value assets.

Initially, financial sponsors used continuation vehicles to hold on to promising assets they believed needed more time to mature. In recent years, the focus has shifted to keeping high-performing, income-generating properties.

Continuation vehicles now comprise nearly 10% of private-equity exits, according to Paine, who said KeyCorp has been looking to add this skill set to its capital-markets tool kit the past few years. 

"As we looked at these businesses and really felt like we could bring that capability to private-equity firms we serve … we just needed to find the right [partner],'' Paine said. "We believe Atlantic-Pacific is the right one." 

Continuation vehicles will likely prove useful outside of the private-equity business — particularly in private-credit specialty finance and real estate — Paine said.

Key's move into continuation vehicles comes as middle-market merger-and-acquisition activity, which has been a historic pillar of the bank's capital-markets revenue stream, has slowed. 

"I would characterize the current environment, certainly for the middle-market and from an M&A standpoint, as not very good," Paine said. "Announced middle-market M&A activity is down 11% in 2026, and it was down the last two years. It's still not picked up."

Still, Key remains firmly on track to reach its goal of collecting $1 billion in annual capital markets revenue by 2028, Paine said.

"I've no worries we won't achieve it, even in the environment we're in right now," Paine said. 

More deals a possibility

Prior to 2026, Key hadn't made a capital-markets acquisition since 2017, when it bought Cain Brothers. Now it's made two such deals in short order.

"We have a strong team supporting both transactions," Paine said in the interview. "While acquisitions always require significant effort, we view both of these transactions as highly manageable and well within our capabilities."

Read more:

  • Fintech target small business niche banks have spurned
  • Revolut wins US charter with limits on four products
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026
  • Jack Henry refuses to pay extortionists after data theft

Paine did not rule out further capital-markets deals. 
"We will continue to look at these good, tuck-in acquisitions," he said Thursday at the industry conference. "There have been quite a few opportunities over the past 24 months. I'm sure there will be more."

Key's deal for Clearwater came after six years of close collaboration between the two companies. There was no similar relationship with Atlantic-Pacific.

Rather, Key said it was attracted to Atlantic-Pacific's strong reputation. Since its founding in 1995, Atlantic-Pacific has executed more than 180 transactions, raising about $123 billion in capital.

Atlantic-Pacific founder and Chairman James Manley said the merger with Key will combine his firm's boutique level of service with the scale and resources of a major regional bank.

"We share a commitment to serving financial sponsors and their investors, and we are excited to build on that foundation together as part of Key," Manley said in a press release.

data.title: Waters teases housing focus on HFSC
data.description:
• Key insight: Waters said that housing would be a priority for the panel under her leadership. 
  • What's at stake: She listed deposit insurance reform and AI bills as potential legislative targets. 

WASHINGTON — Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., promised to focus more keenly on housing on the House Financial Services Committee if she returns as its chair in a five page letter shared with colleagues in a detailed preview of her focus atop the committee. 

Waters faces a challenge to her leadership on the panel, which she has chaired previously, from Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill. In a dear colleague letter, designed to convince her caucus to vote for her to continue leading the committee, Waters outlined her plans for the panel in the future. 

Notably those plans include renaming the committee the Committee on Housing and Financial Services in order to "put housing first." On the housing front, Water said she would work on "expanding affordable housing programs and reforming mortgage finance." 

Mortgage finance is an area where banks, many of which have left the mortgage industry after the 2008 financial crisis, might find common ground with Waters. 

She also promised to create new leadership positions for junior members, including a committee whip, a freshman representative and committee messenger.

Her list of priorities includes a number of old favorites from the senior lawmaker. She said she would eliminate "junk" fees like overdraft fees, restore the independence of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and protect the Community Reinvestment Act and other civil rights era legislation. 

On community banking, Waters said she would help the industry by reforming deposit insurance and support Community Development Financial Institutions and Minority Owned Institutions. 

She added oversight of prediction markets and the Trump administration's crypto dealings to her docket, and said that she would pursue legislation to "AI proof" the economy. She also said she would "expand" access to Federal Reserve master accounts, and would reform the central bank " from its governance to its discount window lending." 

Although Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, Waters has little ability to pass partisan legislation into law with President Donald Trump wielding veto power in the White House. 

But Waters is known as a dealmaker, despite her progressive brand, and has many friends across the aisle, including current Chair French Hill, R-Ark., with whom she's worked on a number of legislative packages, including this Congress' housing bill.

Casten's letter is thinner on specifics, and he faces a tougher road to be elected chair of the committee. He said in his dear colleague letter that "the American people have made clear that the status quo is not sufficient."

data.title: Affirm's direct pitch to bank customers moves forward
data.description:
• Key insight: Affirm is planning to pilot Affirm Edge with banks in the first half of next year.  
  • What's at stake: Edge integrates into banks and credit unions' mobile banking applications, allowing financial institutions to offer buy now, pay later and installment lending directly to their customers. 

Affirm is moving ahead with a long-awaited product that connects its buy now/pay later and installment lending directly to banks' customers. 

Testing for the product, called Affirm Edge, will start in the first half of 2027. Affirm first spoke about Edge at its investor day in May. Bank customers engage with Affirm in their banking app, see their purchasing power and browse the Affirm's marketplace. Affirm plans to originate and service the loans. 

"It's a chance for us to distribute what we know is a better way for consumers to access credit to a really very wide audience by partnering with the issuers of debit cards across banks of all sizes," Michael Linford, Affirm's president, said on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call. 

Progress has been slow-going. "Patience is the code word here," Linford said. "We have a set of partners, both the platform partners as well as the end customers here who don't move exceptionally fast."

Banks and credit unions represent an important distribution channel for Affirm. The company estimated in May that Edge's total addressable market is about $140 billion. Affirm already has its BNPL options embedded into FIS and Fiserv-issued debit cards, and in-app visibility would give it a direct — and trusted line — to banks' customers. 

Affirm did not comment on the general size of the institutions that would be participating in the pilot, but $74-billion-asset Old National Bank in May said during Affirm's investor day in May that the bank was exploring using Edge because its customers were already using BNPL, and offering the credit product would help keep transactions in-house and develop deeper relationships with its customer base.  

Many banks have warmed up to buy now, pay later. U.S. Bank built its own BNPL program, DR Bank, a Darien, Connecticut-based digital bank, works with ClarityPay to offer an embedded lending solution that focuses on travel, elective health, retail and home improvement, and Flint, Michigan-based Financial Plus Credit Union has BNPL embedded into its debit cards through a partnership with white-label provider Equipifi. And many of the major credit card issuers have their own version of post-purchase pay later options available for credit card purchases that exceed specific transaction amounts. 

Affirm is looking to both Edge and the agentic commerce as key growth avenues, according to William Blair analyst Andrew Jeffrey. 

"Affirm is delivering [gross merchandise volume] growth above its 25% medium-term target before potential benefits from Edge and agentic," Jeffrey said in a research note. 

GMW increased 34% year over year to $14.4 billion, the company's 12th consecutive quarter of GMV growth north of 30%. Revenue increased 35% to $1.26 billion. 

Active customers rose 19% to 28.7 million, and transactions per active customer increased to 7.3 per year. Active Affirm Card cardholders hit 6 million, more than double compared to a year ago, and active merchants increased 48% to about 621,000.

data.title: Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
data.description:
• Key insight: The midterm elections reshaped state attorney-general offices, with Democrats now commanding a 29-to-22 majority.
  • Forward look: State AGs are expected to aggressively target big-tech companies, algorithmic-pricing schemes and AI privacy risks. 

After flipping five Republican seats in Tuesday's election, Democratic attorneys general are entrenching themselves in the role they started filling last year: serving as a counterweight to hollowed-out federal enforcement under President Trump.

The trend could be especially noticeable in the consumer-protection realm, where Democrats see a particular void. During the second Trump administration, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has been shedding staff and conducting almost no enforcement of the relevant laws, experts say.

Starting early next year, Democrats will hold a 29-to-22 majority in AG offices for the 50 states and the District of Columbia. On Tuesday, they captured Republican-held seats in Georgia, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas, defeating GOP incumbents in the latter two states. 

Incoming AGs are already looking to build their leadership teams and consumer-protection units — even recruiting former CFPB enforcement attorneys to bolster their ranks. 

"They're going to ramp up fairly quickly," Michael Yaghi, a litigation partner at Troutman Pepper Locke who specializes in state attorneys general and regulations, told American Banker. 

"There's going to be a lot of pressure on all 29 of these Democratic AGs to continue to push back against the Trump administration," said Sarah Mercer, a lawyer and lobbyist at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, speaking on a webinar Thursday.

Democratic AGs are expected to heed the will of voters by focusing on pocketbook issues, including price gouging, hidden fees and algorithmic pricing, which is sometimes called dynamic pricing.

Several states, including Maryland, Connecticut and New Jersey, have passed new laws to restrict "surveillance pricing" — where companies use personal data to set individualized prices.

In the financial-services realm, lenders could face more pressure to provide consumers with clear disclosures, so they understand the all-in price of what they are financing.

Former Sen. Mark Pryor, a Democrat who also served as Arkansas' attorney general from 1999 to 2003, said the states will be looking for ways to address pocketbook issues.

"One area where I think [the states] have been very directly involved in affordability in the last year is dynamic pricing," Pryor said Thursday, speaking on a webinar focused on the changeover in state AG offices,

Pryor also pointed to artificial intelligence as an area of keen interest.

"I think you'll continue to see the attorneys general look at AI issues, especially around children and also around consumer protection," he said. 

State AGs will likely be scrutinizing how companies deploy AI, as well as their automated pricing algorithms, to ensure that digital tools don't obscure true costs from consumers. Another area of potential AI-related scrutiny: the rapid expansion of data centers that have drawn a significant public backlash.

The scrutiny will not be coming only from Democrats. With a total of 14 fresh faces stepping into state AG offices, experts see the potential for bipartisan coalitions to tackle cost-of-living issues, predatory pricing and the intersection of AI and commerce. 

Former Colorado Attorney General John Suthers, a Republican who has also served as the U.S. Attorney for Colorado and is a former mayor of Colorado Springs, said state AGs may form unlikely alliances in the next two years to address antitrust issues. 

"We're going to see a higher level of cooperation between Republicans and Democrats at the industry-watchdog level," Suthers said. "Democrats will be concerned about corporate mergers, and everybody will be concerned about data privacy and social media."

The pullback in federal enforcement has spurred states to fill the void.

"When Congress or D.C. isn't functioning well, AGs oftentimes step in," Pryor said. "If we're going to look at the next two years, it's very possible that Washington won't be functioning very well, and so you could think that AGs might step in." 

Broad, bipartisan coalitions of state attorneys general have recently joined forces to target major financial and fintech firms. This year alone, a coalition of 18 state AGs targeted Capital One Financial for deceiving 360 Savings account holders; 46 AGs took action against Block for failing to protect users from fraud on its CashApp payment platform; and 41 AGs pursued subprime auto lender Credit Acceptance Corp. for trapping low-income car buyers in risky loans they couldn't afford.  

The states also have big-tech companies in their sights. 

In August, a bipartisan coalition of 52 attorneys general reached an $18.6 billion-dollar settlement with Meta Platforms. The deal resolved long-standing litigation alleging that Meta knowingly designed features on Facebook and Instagram that were addictive and harmed children and teenagers.

The new crop of state AGs are likely to take a different approach than the Federal Trade Commission, which has become the most active federal regulator under the Trump administration.

While the FTC has been focused on providing restitution for concerns who were harmed, energized state AGs are looking to leverage state-level consumer-protection statutes to push for significant penalties and injunctive relief Injunctive that requires changes to their business practices, Yaghi said.

"States are going to be more aggressive in terms of not only how companies are harming consumers, but also on what their business model looks like and how they can change the way a company operates to help protect consumers," Yaghi told American Banker. "They want civil penalties and want to fundamentally alter how companies promote products, market services, and operate their day-to-day business."

In past periods of deregulation in Washington, state AGs have tended to step forward to fill the gap.

"There's also this idea of 'underreach,' where the federal government should be doing certain things — there are federal responsibilities around antitrust. And if the state agencies feel like the Feds are not holding up their end in the market, that's when the state agencies may come in and try to fill that," Pryor said.

Because state AGs can stack multiple violations on top of one another to pile on steep civil penalties, companies should consider proactive auditing, Yaghi said.

"Now is a good time for companies to double-check how they are using and deploying AI, setting prices and disclosing and advertising products and services," he said.

data.title: 'Friendly fraud' isn't so friendly. Here's how banks can fight back
data.description:
• Key insight: First-party fraud is on the rise and could get worse as agentic commerce grows.
  • Expert quote: "It's a big area of concern for banks, right after what's happening in agentic use of AI by fraudsters."---Datos' Jim Mortensen.

Instances of individuals knowingly disputing legitimate transactions are ratcheting up. Banks need to batten down the hatches or risk greater exposure to what's known as friendly fraud, or first-party fraud. 

Global card-related first-party fraud is expected to cost financial institutions and merchants $4.8 billion in 2028, up from an estimated $3.9 billion in 2025, according to a report from Datos Insights. Between 2023 and 2024, 35% of FIs and 64% of merchants reported year-over-year increases in card-related first-party fraud.

The problem is likely more acute than these estimates suggest. That's because Datos' estimates don't include variables such as losses from account and credit-level fraud, noncard payments, and operational overhead that results from processing these claims. And it stands to get worse as agentic commerce proliferates.

"It's a big area of concern for banks, right after what's happening in agentic use of AI by fraudsters," Jim Mortensen, strategic advisor in the fraud and AML practice at Datos, told American Banker.

Here's what banks need to know about the latest trends in first-party fraud:

All hands on deck

Merchants, banks, card brands, and fintechs are focusing on solutions to reduce fraud. 

Mastercard's First-Party Trust program has been in the U.S. since 2024, and the card brand recently expanded its rollout to parts of Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Mastercard First-Party Trust helps merchants and issuers more accurately distinguish genuine fraud from first-party misuse. Visa has its own program: Compelling Evidence 3.0. 

"Merchants and issuers estimate that approximately 20% of disputes are linked to first-party fraud, making it one of the largest contributors to preventable chargebacks today," Mastercard wrote in a blog.

Additionally, more commercial platforms, designed to address first-party fraud, are coming to market. These solutions help banks approach fraud more holistically rather than transactionally, often using AI. 

What are banks doing wrong?

Taking a transactional-only approach can miss many instances of fraud. Fraud rings are prevalent, and they try to bring more people into the fold, often through social media. 

"We're seeing a lot of big accounts on TikTok that get removed and people arrested because of what they're posting," Soups Ranjan, co-founder and chief executive of Sardine, an AI risk platform for fraud, told American Banker. "Because of that, there's been a shift toward videos of people holding stacks of cash and talking about investing or getting business credit. Then they direct people off-platform to discuss specifics."

Banks that focus primarily on transactional data can easily miss rings of criminal activity. Ranjan offers the hypothetical example of multiple chargebacks that are seemingly dissimilar: One for $25, another for $26, and the other for $27. They are all from different merchants. On the surface, there's no apparent connection. Digging deeper, however, it could become clear they all signed up for their cards in the same city around the same time, and there might be other connections as well. 

Individually, the fraudulent charges are often low, but collectively, there can be large losses. "Fraud is a data-science problem," Ranjan told American Banker. "You need to detect fraud rings who are doing this at scale."

Context matters

Many banks don't look at claims with enough context, according to Suzanne Sando, lead analyst of fraud management at Javelin Strategy & Research. "They don't have sufficient data to determine whether or not they should move forward with the chargeback," Sando told American Banker. If you don't have access to the right data or are not in a position to piece some of the data points together, "you're already missing a big piece of the puzzle," she said. Having this data "helps you confirm real abuse or a suspicion."

James Hunt, a product strategy professional at Feedzai, a fraud prevention and detection company, offered a real-life example of how banks are using technology for this purpose.

Read more:

  • Bankers swing to negative view on funding costs: Survey
  • How agentic commerce is changing the customer experience
  • Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
  • $6B Binance heist provokes stablecoin freeze dilemma

A consumer had made several transactions to a retailer between June and September totaling around $700. None of these had been disputed by the cardholder. A transaction was then made during a sale period in early October to the same retailer for roughly $500, which the consumer disputed a few weeks later.While it's very challenging for an issuer to distinguish between deliberate exploitation, customer confusion, and merchant non-delivery, in this case, non-delivery was unlikely given that it was a major name-brand retailer with a consistent history of delivery to this customer. In addition, in this scenario, the bank was monitoring the customer's credit card and regular checking account. The customer was low on cash at the time of the purchase, indicating a potential financial crunch. "This is often a trigger for good customers to abuse the dispute process," Hunt said.
While this isn't proof of fraud, having all this data allows a bank to probe further and "take appropriate action to protect their relationship with both the consumer and card networks," Hunt said.

The problem is likely to get worse

Sando predicted that first-party fraud will become more of an issue as agentic commerce enters the mainstream. As consumers get more comfortable with agentic commerce, fraud claims are expected to rise—at least initially. Some may be legitimate claims, but some people will try to claim they didn't authorize the agent when they really did, she told American Banker. 

That's where agent trust models become so important in identifying first-party fraud. Audit logs, coupled with transaction history and dispute patterns, can build a stronger picture of whether it's a legitimate dispute or an attempt to defraud, she told American Banker. "The most important thing here is understanding the intent of the purchase."

data.title: Why banks are searching for value in AI investments
data.description:
How are banks looking at new and ongoing AI investments? Kirti Choudhary and Vikram Sivakumar, both managing directors and partners at consulting firm BCG, sit down with Chana Schoenberger, Editor-in-Chief of American Banker, to discuss.

Transcription:


Chana Schoenberger (00:09):

Hi, I'm Chana Schoenberger. I'm the editor-in-chief of American Banker, and I'm here with two managing directors and partners from BCG, Kirti Choudhury and Vikram Sivakumar. Welcome.

Vikram Sivakumar (00:20):

Thank you.

Kirti Choudhary (00:21):

Thank you.

Chana Schoenberger (00:22):

So you deal a lot with banks and AI. Can you tell me what clients are asking you about right now in the AI space?

Kirti Choudhary (00:30):

I think right now the conversation has really moved to value. We are investing a lot of time, capacity, as well as dollars behind this. Where is the value? The second bit is a lot around what are some big ticket investments and where do we really focus our attention to scale this and to really bring customers as well as employees a lot of new refined experiences, remove toil and bring joy.

Chana Schoenberger (00:58):

Joy from our jobs? Absolutely.

Kirti Choudhary (00:59):

At

Chana Schoenberger (01:00):

A bank?

Vikram Sivakumar (01:02):

Okay. I think very much the same. Usually three parts of the conversation. Value, how do I run this program to actually get value out the door? And third on, what are the foundational pieces that I have or don't have that I should be putting in place so I can do this well? So how do I build up the missionary inside of the bank to actually deliver the value, point me in the right direction, and then organize me in a way that I can get it out the door?

Chana Schoenberger (01:25):

I feel like a lot of companies right now are installing pieces of AI and they're integrating it into varying workflows, but there isn't often a lot of measurement built in.

Kirti Choudhary (01:36):

The way we have typically seen measurement is along, I would say, a few different paradigms. There's obviously the financial side of things. So you're looking at anything from productivity, how much things are costing, whether it is on a per widget basis and/or from per experience basis. You then start to get into growth. Are you able to truly deepen relationships with your customers? The other side of this then is also non-financial outcomes. So everything from, hey, are controls performing better to what is the satisfaction which either employees have or customers have? So I'd say it's truly multidimensional in terms of how we start to see and measure the value from these things.

Vikram Sivakumar (02:16):

Maybe to add some contrarian thoughts, the running joke in my family is I've got the Peloton, I have a series of widgets, I wear a band, I wear a glucose monitor and I haven't lost weight. And so I think the value conversation is important, but getting into making the change matters just as much. And I know we're having a lot of the value conversations and we should. We should talk about the inputs, outputs and outcomes, but I do see companies getting stuck in that conversation about what is the perfect metric. There doesn't exist one all the time. We've got to find a few and move on with it, but then we've got to jump into the action itself. A roundabout answer, but just a reality check.

Chana Schoenberger (02:53):

Something I've heard from banking executives recently is there's this problem that the models are getting better and better and better. And so there's a bit of a reluctance to commit to one model or one piece of software or one feature because you know that whatever you build to now, it's going to be even better later and then you're going to feel like you wasted time and money. What do you do about that?

Kirti Choudhary (03:16):

I think a lot of this is just about beginning in some cases. I think in many ways there are a lot of simple things which bank can start to get, right? So whether it is customers trying to make simple transactions or get help with simple queries, frankly, you don't need a lot of model intelligence or advancements to do that. So I would almost encourage people to reframe the problem a little bit. It's less about models and what you want out of it. It's more about what experiences are you trying to fix? What are almost changes or increments you can make to that experience? What are things which current models can do and do well? And what are things which truly need to be reshaped or rethough of from the get-go? It's a little bit of cutting the problem in parts and dealing with it versus necessarily saying we're going to wait forever or we're going to build something very advanced.

Vikram Sivakumar (04:09):

I think there's a lot of investments that are necessarily foundational that will also be needed when the model gets better. One part of that is the human side of it. Many other parts of that are things like data, how do you govern AI? I think getting through that and doing the work is the only way that the org can make that transformation. And so we can wait for the best tool to come through, but we've got to get started on arguably places that we know we're going to get benefit and where we will have to do the work to get through that hump. We're not talking about AI across 100% of the bank, but there are pieces of the bank that we will get value and we've just got to get the piece started.

Kirti Choudhary (04:49):

The one thing I would add to that is also I think increasingly there is also messaging and signal value. What do you tell your investors? What do you tell your employees? What do you tell your customers? And in many cases, not doing anything is also a signal which we start to send out.

Chana Schoenberger (05:07):

Right. You have to signal that you're a forward thinking institution.

data.title: How bank execs are leading the charge for AI
data.description:
CEOs and their senior leaders are now driving the charge for AI adoption within banks to fight fraud and find profits in new ways. Kirti Choudhary and Vikram Sivakumar, both managing directors and partners at consulting firm BCG, discussed this with Chana Schoenberger, Editor-in-Chief of American Banker.

Transcription:


Chana Schoenberger (00:09):

I did have one executive tell me recently that he'd had a conversation and the upshot of it was the amount of money that you're getting out of efficiency from AI, you then have to put back into fighting fraud and cybersecurity problems from bad AI actors. Are you seeing any of that?

Vikram Sivakumar (00:30):

More and more a conversation top of the house, particularly with the mythos conversations coming through. I think more of it, I think with the agents that are coming into market as well, you're going to end up seeing more of it. I think the linking of the two is a bit interesting. You will have to make that investment whether you're investing in your own AI capabilities or not. You still need to secure up the boundaries.

Kirti Choudhary (00:53):

I think it's a bit of a balance, right? If you sort of rewind 20, 25 years when digital had first started, and there were a lot of instances where yes, people are getting benefits, but you had different types of digital fraud which was happening. I think there might be a point at which productivity will win, a point at which fraud might win. But I'd say again, in 15, 20 years when some of this becomes the new normal, we will settle at a new equilibrium.

Chana Schoenberger (01:22):

Is there something that you think banks will sort of automatically be doing with AI next year that they're not doing now?

Vikram Sivakumar (01:31):

Wish we knew. I mean, good billion dollar question at this point. Look, I think a lot of banks, at least over the last couple of years, have come to certain areas of bets that everyone is starting to make. And the top of the house has started to prioritize it much more than say two years ago where it was probably tech led or an engineer led. That shift has definitely happened. That also means many of the banks are focusing on a few big rocks and where they want to go. And so I think that doubling down on few places and making those shifts from the tool to the org changing and how the ways are working changing are things that are going to play out. I don't think the tools have completely gotten to the change in what a human does day to day, and that I would expect to see a lot more of going into next year.

(02:20):

Both the security and cost conversations have started and I think they will also mature a lot more going into the next year.

Kirti Choudhary (02:29):

What I'd add to that is first, I think risk governance and tolerances will start to become a lot clearer. So both in terms of customer facing and internal facing and third party facing, we will have a set of policies, procedures, as well as tolerances, which will be clearly laid out. The second one, just to echo what Wikram said, no regrets use cases will become pretty clear. So when it comes to fraud, when it comes to cyber, when it comes to customer service, when it comes to engineering, there'd be a couple of areas where this starts to become just omnipresent and almost everyone will start to follow because there will be too many scaled cases which are available. And third, I think we'll move from a thousand flowers bloom approach to a few big bets people start to make. And we do expect there might be fintechs and potential players who might start experimenting with changing the business model itself.

data.title: How regulation could change AI adoption at banks
data.description:
As fintechs are granted bank charters, the boundary between banks and fintechs gets more porous, and regulation becomes more important. Kirti Choudhary and Vikram Sivakumar, both managing directors and partners at consulting firm BCG, sat down to a conversation about this with Chana Schoenberger, Editor-in-Chief of American Banker.

Transcription:


Chana Schoenberger (00:09):

And how does regulation fit into all of this? That of course is the bright line between a bank and a fintech.

Kirti Choudhary (00:15):

That one actually increasingly is sort of, again, one of the key questions. I think this year has been marquee in that you've had a large number of fintechs getting banking charters. So they will experience what it feels like to be regulated. Many would say it's sort of leveling the playing field a little bit, but I do think what it also signals is the potential cost of putting the harnesses in place and/or complying itself might become easier due to which you're finding a lower payers wanting to enter. It also potentially means that they do want to experiment with changing some of the business models. So I think time will tell where and how it shakes out, but just the number of new banks we're going to have in the next few years will be pretty telling.

Vikram Sivakumar (01:08):

I think we talk a lot about the regulators from the financial sector. I think we're also going to need to talk about the regulators from an AI perspective on its own. And that's a conversation that's also maturing. And so they will meet at some point, but it's also coming.

Chana Schoenberger (01:24):

Well, that's assuming that the government starts regulating AI in some -

Vikram Sivakumar (01:28):

Shape or form.

Chana Schoenberger (01:29):

Regular way.

Vikram Sivakumar (01:30):

It's a conversation and if not a regulation, maybe a standard, but it's a conversation that's playing out. And as banks, we're probably watching both of those.

Kirti Choudhary (01:39):

I think there's also the question though of one, we have banks which are just local, but there are many large institutions which operate in multiple geographies and they will certainly have more of this to watch out for.

Chana Schoenberger (01:53):

Definitely.

data.title: The human challenge to AI adoption at banks
data.description:
Bank workers are afraid of AI and what it might mean for their jobs. Execs have to overcome these concerns to get the benefits of AI within the bank. Kirti Choudhary and Vikram Sivakumar, both managing directors and partners at consulting firm BCG, discussed this with Chana Schoenberger, Editor-in-Chief of American Banker.

Transcription:


Chana Schoenberger (00:09):

What about the risks? What are the biggest risks you see right now for AI in the sector?

Vikram Sivakumar (00:14):

Where should we begin? Banks are very good at managing risks by nature. I mean, that's why I bank with a bank. The conversation started at the trust level. So maintaining my brand and my trust with customers is kind of paramount to it. And I think it's a conversation that is... When you talk about AI, it's not about how do I operate at speed and safely, it's about how do I operate safely and at speed in that order. And so trust is a big part of the risk that we talked through. The other side of it is the competitive lens of it, which is the inaction is also a risk of some form. And so how do we balance that? Look, I think banks do that better than most people in the world, and that's one that they've managed for many, many years and just a new muscle to learn and completely expect them to do that.

Kirti Choudhary (01:05):

I'd say overall agree with Bikram. Risk management is sort of first nature to banks. I do think there's a bit of a questioning around the posture of it, of how do you not be too conservative? At the same time, how do you anticipate different items and how do you not treat AI and models that it needs to sit above how a human would behave or an employee would behave in that same setting? I'd say in terms of specific areas where there is a lot more thought given is potentially cyber threats, fraud, increasingly third and fourth party risks, and finally just operational risks based on what these models might do when they become customer facing or bot facing.

Chana Schoenberger (01:50):

Yeah. There's this whole question of what happens when my agent talks to the bank's agent and there is a human somewhere, but the humans are not so involved.

Kirti Choudhary (02:02):

And I think there's a big liability question there as well, but part of this is we can either first try and solve every question in every edge case, or we can run some experiments, see how things shake out, learn from it and make some progress.

Chana Schoenberger (02:19):

Tell me about how the human side is involved here. Obviously banks are people.

Vikram Sivakumar (02:23):

100%. I think it's the crux of the challenge. We can get the tools out and then we've got to get the change done over a period of time. It is one that we are coming to grapple with. It is one that we are starting to recognize as the change management issue, but one where the playbook is not necessarily fully available for everyone to play out with. When I go in, we do a lot of work around the change management aspect and we start with a survey and there's always three concerns that come up from the folks and the three concerns are in different orders, but always the same three. I'm afraid of losing my job. I don't trust AI and I don't have time to learn. And solving that therefore is both a conversation about how do you create that structured approach and environment for a team to learn and behave in a new way, but also showing them that they have a job at the end of that transformation.

(03:15):

It isn't about taking their job away. There's also a part of the leadership conversation we need to have, which is how do you model the change and not mandate it when you're in a town hall and if you're asked what is your favorite use case, you can actually talk about it in authenticity and in detail. So it's a change both for the ground, but also both middle management and top management about taking the org along on that journey. More and more, I think the last part of it is that boards are also starting to ask organizations about what is that pathway for the rest with the post AI era? How are we responsibly taking care of our talent? What does that mean from both an upskilling, re-skilling pathway rather than a, hey, we got here and we don't need people anymore. So that's a more of a mature conversation that the workforce transformation itself is one that we're hearing more about and we need to talk a lot more explicitly about.

Kirti Choudhary (04:05):

I think the piece I would add there is just culture and culture is just so important to organizations to both in which how do leaders signal that they're AI first institutions that they want to make progress, but they want to make progress not at the cost of humans, but taking humans along on the journey. And in many ways, how do they signal and build that culture where organizations start to rally behind it? And again, don't think that they're being replaced, but think that they're being augmented and that there will be new jobs which are needed in the AI era.

Chana Schoenberger (04:46):

Great. Great. Well, thank you so much for coming in. I really appreciate it.

Vikram Sivakumar (04:50):

Thanks for having us.

Kirti Choudhary (04:51):

Thank you.

data.title: Strong jobs report keeps Fed focus squarely on inflation
data.description:
• Key insight: Underlying economic growth remains strong, likely giving the Federal Open Market Committee the freedom to increase interest rates to tame inflation.
  • Expert quote: "The jobless rate is lower than a year ago, and payroll growth is noticeably above last year's pace. The four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims continues to run at the lowest level in generations. So on the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive." —Fed Chair Kevin Warsh

Inflation is overtaking unemployment as the top priority for the Federal Reserve in light of a stronger-than-expected October jobs report.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics released its monthly report on Friday morning, showing an uptick of 165,000 jobs last month dropping the unemployment rate from 4.2% to 4.1%.

The strong reading surpassed consensus forecasts, which had called for a gain of 65,000 jobs and was well above the average monthly gain of the past year of 48,000. The report revised estimates from the past two months, adding 31,000 to September's tepid 29,000 reading and adding another 53,000 to August's already strong 133,000 total. 

The report is the first major economic indicator released since last week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which the group opted to hold interest rates steady between 3.75% and 4%. 

The BLS report alone does little to change the Fed's outlook on the economy, which for months has been squarely focused on persistently high inflation rather than the health of the labor market.

"The jobless rate is lower than a year ago, and payroll growth is noticeably above last year's pace," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said during his post FOMC press conference last week. "The four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims continues to run at the lowest level in generations. So on the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive."

Read more:

  • Wall Street critic Sherrod Brown heads back to Senate
  • Swipe fee bill cosponsor Marshall defeated in reelection
  • Roy Cooper flips bank-heavy North Carolina
  • Bank advocate Andy Barr clinches Kentucky Senate seat

The Fed's preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures index from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, showed prices growing at 3.6% in September, well above the Fed's 2% target. With the jobs report demonstrating the strength of the labor market and overall economy, the Fed has no economic impediment to raising rates to tame inflation. 

Market participants broadly expect the Fed to raise its benchmark rate next month during its final meeting of 2026, with 75% of federal funds futures contracts reflecting a quarter-percentage-point increase, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

FOMC participants have offered little in the way of guidance this week, likely the result of policymakers steering clear of commentary around the midterm elections. 

One committee member who has offered her latest analysis is Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack, one of the two dissenting voters to last week's FOMC decision. Hammock and Fed Gov. Lisa Cook both voted against the decision, preferring instead that the committee increase interest rates to address persistently high inflation. 

"I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said Thursday at an event in Zurich, adding she prefers making "more frequent, smaller adjustments when possible."

The unemployment rate has been between 4.1% and 4.3% since March. During that time, monthly jobs reports have varied from six figure increases like October to slight declines. Monthly readings have also been subject to significant revisions, a change that policymakers attribute to the tight job market and stagnant population growth. 

The next major economic indicator for the Fed will come next week, when the BLS releases its October consumer price index report on Tuesday.

data.title: BankThink Can the US catch up to the rest of the G7 on payments modernization?
data.description:
• Key insight: The U.S. is the only G7 country that hasn't extended direct access to the payments system to nonbanks. This raises costs for consumers and stifles innovation, particularly in cross-border payments.
  • Supporting data: In 2025, people and businesses moved about $43 trillion across borders.

International money movement is a crucial part of the global economy. In 2025, people and businesses moved about $43 trillion across borders. However, international payments remain slower, more expensive and less transparent than domestic payments. This friction inflates the cost of international trade and hurts broader economic growth.

The G20 set out a Roadmap for Enhancing Cross-Border Payments to tackle the challenges of international payments. In response, many countries have made progress toward modernizing payment systems and allowing regulated nonbank institutions to connect to them directly. That's because direct access to local payments systems can reduce payment processing costs by up to 10x, allowing everyday people and businesses to move money globally in a faster and more affordable way.

The U.S. has made advances in payments modernization, including the launch of the retail instant payment system FedNow in 2023. But it remains the only G7 country that has not expanded direct access to its local payments systems beyond banks. This limitation stops nonbank institutions, like money transmitters that provide payment services, from being eligible to connect directly to the infrastructure that processes the movement of dollars.

The White House, policymakers in Congress and the Federal Reserve have all taken important steps to widen access to the American payment rails. In particular, the proposed Payment Account is an advancement in the right direction, but it still excludes nonbank institutions and imposes limitations on key services, such as FedACH, the most used rail for digital payments.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • EWA fintech EarnIn evokes the Constitution in fight over tips
  • Block claims it can replace merchants' vendors with AI
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, in turn, is going further. Rather than forcing all institutions seeking a federal charter to become a full-service bank, the OCC uses the breadth of its legal authority to bring relevant institutions under its regulatory perimeter based on the activities they perform and the risks they create. By adopting this approach, the OCC promotes competition while preserving stability.
Ultimately, nonbank institutions should not be denied a federal licensing pathway simply because they do not take deposits or make loans. As federal law explicitly allows the OCC to charter national banks with special or limited purpose, the legal pathway is and should remain open. Otherwise, institutions seeking to directly access local rails will not even be able to take the first step toward that goal.

Ideally, the OCC's policy position will inspire a broader interpretation of the existing rules governing direct access to payment rails through an account at the Federal Reserve. Many countries have been successful doing this through a risk-based criteria based on the business model of nonbank institutions. And the key here is that, when nonbanks meet the regulatory standards, access to payment infrastructure must be an option. And right now, that's not the case in the U.S.

The OCC's stance, along with recent initiatives from the White House and Congress, is well aligned with the priorities set by the G20 to enhance cross-border payments by 2027 and shows that the U.S. can get back to leading the world in payments modernization. Let's not waste this opportunity.

data.title: What AI agents can do for banks' customer relationships
data.description:
• Key insight: Some banks are using AI to improve their relationships with small businesses.
  • Expert quote: "We're not looking for it to go out and contact our customers, because that is the core of who we say we are. We're looking for ways that we can utilize it in-house that will create efficiencies so that we can do a better job of being in front of our customer."—Cristin Reid, CEO of Capitol National Bank

The next wave of artificial intelligence offers promises of autonomous agents for banks to deploy across different departments. For small business-focused banks, agentic AI is presenting both challenges and opportunities for relationship managers as they work to serve their business clients better.
"Many of the opportunities lie around the democratization and the accessibility of data that AI creates," Michael Desimone, chief banking and lending officer at Citadel Federal Credit Union, said during a panel at American Banker's Small Business Banking conference last week. "It's all out there for us, but it's sort of unmanageable and hard to get your arms around. The ability to not spend hours pouring over research and memos to have a good, solid understanding of what a business needs, what it does and where it fits in its segment is very valuable."

The raw internal data a bank typically has at its disposal often needs to be identified, sorted and curated to determine what is relevant, according to Gary Class, global industry strategist for analytics firm Teradata. Both the company and its bank customers have been using agentic AI to improve the efficiency of data clean-up, he said.

"That can be a very painful process, and that's one thing where agentic AI has really come to the fore," he said.

Capitol National Bank CEO Cristin Reid said that small banks, such as Capitol, aren't necessarily looking for AI agents to take the place of interpersonal relationship building.

"We're not looking for it to go out and contact our customers, because that is the core of who we say we are," she said. "We're looking for ways that we can utilize it in-house that will create efficiencies so that we can do a better job of being in front of our customer."

Reid explained that Capitol is currently bringing agentic AI to back-office operations such as BSA and AML detection, and is developing a deposit attrition model that can flag at-risk customers to relationship managers. 

"It will integrate our core system and pull information about each one of our customers and their deposit activity," she said. "Are their transactions staying the same? Did they change their address? Did they stop a recurring deposit that's going in? What are the key indicators that could hint to us that they're considering going to another bank or moving? It will rank those customers based on risk, then it talks directly to the CRM model. That's going to put the emphasis for us on maintaining that relationship."

Desimone noted that bank regulations need to rapidly evolve around agentic AI models.

"If you think back over places where regulators have had to adapt, it's usually after some kind of a crisis or when something material goes awry," he said. "There's been small instances of that but no major ones yet. We're going to learn on the fly, and someone will be the sacrificial organization that we all learn from because things don't go well for them. That's harsh, but it's reality."

Reid emphasized that banks can also build their internal governance models with AI in mind from the outset.

"AI can be helpful in so many ways, but it's critically important that you take the time to learn and understand and implement the governance models first," she said. "That's going to give you a lot of answers as to whether it's going to work within your organization or not. We're very excited about those opportunities, but we're moving very cautiously so we don't inadvertently step on a landmine [by] not understanding our risks or our partner's guardrails."

Reid emphasized that at her bank, employees will remain at the forefront of customer relationships.

"I don't believe human relationships are going away, even if AI is incredibly successful," Reid said. "What we have to work on is creating that opportunity to enhance those human relationships rather than to minimize them."

data.title: Court ruling makes lower swipe fees likely, not imminent
data.description:
• Key insight: New court precedents have made defending the Fed's 2011 rule an uphill battle, but the Fed still has a lot to fight for: namely its discretion in crafting future policies. 
  • Expert quote: "They're already moving towards a lower cap. What I expect them to actually really defend is their discretion over the methodology and which costs count. Updating the number, that's one thing, but accepting a judicial interpretation that would substantially narrow its regulatory authority is quite another." —John Popeo, president of The Gallatin Group

The Federal Reserve has been ordered to lower the cap it imposes on debit interchange fees, but don't expect it to start rewriting its policies anytime soon.

At least one more court must opine on a lawsuit challenging whether or not the Fed's Regulation II is a faithful interpretation of its authorizing law. Then all parties must wait to see if the Supreme Court decides to weigh in. 

If the courts continue to rule against the Fed's current interchange cap — an increasingly likely outcome given recent legal precedent on administrative discretion — whatever replaces it will be more restrictive on debit card-issuing banks with at least $10 billion of assets. But the ramifications for banks could run even deeper if regulators can no longer rationalize regulatory laws in their favor. 

Because of this, some legal and regulatory analysts expect the Fed to emphasize the process that went into crafting Reg II rather than its ultimate result. John Popeo, a former lawyer for the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and president of regulatory advisory firm The Gallatin Group, noted that the Fed was already prepared to lower the cap, putting out a proposal to do so in 2023.

"They're already moving towards a lower cap," Popeo said. "What I expect them to actually really defend is their discretion over the methodology and which costs count. Updating the number, that's one thing, but accepting a judicial interpretation that would substantially narrow its regulatory authority is quite another."

'Regulatory drift'

Last week, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals rendered its decision in Corner Post v. Federal Reserve Board, a 2021 lawsuit challenging the Fed's 2011 rule implementing the Durbin Amendment to the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. The court found that Reg II overstepped the boundaries assigned by the law.

Judge David Stras, writing for the three-judge panel, said the Fed deviated from the statute by factoring non-transaction-specific costs into the cap. He argued that costs are either variable or fixed and, by the letter of the law, issuers could not recoup their fixed cost investments through interchange fees. Yet, he said, the Fed's approach of a 21-cent base fee, a 0.05 basis point ad valorem charge and an optional 1 cent adjustment for fraud-loss mitigation did just that.

"Among the non-transaction-specific costs it included were fixed costs related to authorization, clearance, and settlement; network processing fees; transaction-monitoring costs for fraud prevention, and fraud losses," Stras wrote. "The clearest sign of regulatory drift was the flat 21-cent cap because it applied to every transaction, no matter its cost."

The decision upheld the lower court's ruling, saying, in no uncertain terms, that the central bank must "come up with a fee structure that reflects the statute Congress wrote," namely one that omits costs not tied to specific transactions, as the Durbin Amendment instructs.

"The Fed is simply supposed to do what it's instructed to do. The Fed took significant liberties [under Durbin], but now it's being brought to account," said Eric Grover, principal at Intrepid Ventures, a payments consulting firm. "We're going to see some foot dragging, but ultimately we're going to see the law implemented as intended."

Not open to interpretation

Former Fed General Counsel Scott Alvarez said the Eighth Circuit's ruling might indicate how other administrative law cases will be handled. 

Alvarez pointed to two recent Supreme Court decisions that have set critical precedent for the interchange fee battle. The first is an earlier iteration of Corner Post v. Fed, which expanded the statute of limitations for challenging regulatory changes, and the second is Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which put an end to the decades-old practice of courts granting agencies broad deference to interpret ambiguous legislation.

"The combination of Loper Bright and Corner Post means judges get to decide what they think is best, which will lead to many different interpretations," Alvarez said, noting that the Eighth Circuit decision rested on a black-and-white interpretation of the Durbin Amendment that could reasonably be deemed open to interpretation. "It's a fallacy to say there is only one correct reading of a statute, there are many ways to read them."

Read more:

  • Wall Street critic Sherrod Brown heads back to Senate
  • Swipe fee bill cosponsor Marshall defeated in reelection
  • Roy Cooper flips bank-heavy North Carolina
  • Bank advocate Andy Barr clinches Kentucky Senate seat

Alvarez said this new legal environment could result in less regulatory clarity and heavier involvement of courts in rulemaking processes. 

"You could end up with three different courts interpreting the same statute three different ways. I don't see how anybody lives with that," he said. "Different readings will certainly keep the Supreme Court busy."

Conflicting opinions

Rather than move to swiftly revise its interchange rule based solely on last week's decision, Alvarez said the Fed is likely to wait for the result of another lawsuit, Linney's Pizza v. The Federal Reserve Board, which is winding through the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals. 

In that case, the plaintiff is also claiming that the Fed set the debit interchange cap too high. But, unlike in Corner Post, the district court in this case ruled in favor of the Fed last year, saying the central bank met its legal obligations during the rulemaking process — even in light of the Loper Bright shift away from broad deference. 

If the Fed wins again, the split between the Sixth and Eight circuits would put pressure on the Supreme Court to take up the issue. Given that the composition of the court has not changed since the Loper Bright decision, there is a strong chance it sides with the Eighth Circuit. But, Alvarez noted, the court would also have to contend with a 2015 decision from the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which swatted down an earlier attempt to challenge the legality of the current interchange cap. 

Alvarez said the best course of action for the Fed is to see exactly what framework it will be operating under before committing time and resources to a new rule. 

"I would tend toward not wanting to go forward with the rulemaking with the difference of the two opinions. I'd appeal to the Supreme Court first," he said. "If the Eighth Circuit prevails, the Fed's 2023 proposal totally has to be abandoned and it has to start from scratch. If the DC Circuit prevails, it could move forward with what it has already."

If the Eighth Circuit ruling carries, the Fed could not simply revert to its 2023 proposal, which would have lowered the base fee to 14.4 cents, dropped the ad valorem rate to 0.04 basis points and raised the fraud adjustment to 1.3 cents. Alvarez said the central bank would need to take an entirely different approach, one that hues closer to the actual costs incurred by banks at the time of processing. 

Debit economics

One of the issues the Fed faced in 2011 is that per-transaction costs vary widely from bank to bank. That variance has only been exacerbated over time. Many smaller issuers — including many above the $10 billion exemption cut off — rely on third-party core processors to authorize, clear and settle transactions for them. Because these services are external, it is easy to draw the line between expenses that are related to debit transactions and those that are not.

The largest debit card issuing banks in the country are more likely to build out their own payments infrastructure. This approach generates a lot of up-front costs that dwindle to virtually nothing when spread out over time and across billions of transactions per year.

In 2024, JPMorganChase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo each processed more than half a trillion dollars of debit card transaction volume, spread out across more than 32 billion purchases collectively. According to the Fed's latest national payments volume report, that would translate into roughly a third of the non-prepaid debit card activity from that year. If the cap is revised to reflect the actual per-transaction costs incurred by these banks, not only would they be forced to offset their investment costs in other ways, they would also lose a significant chunk of revenue.

Last year, Wells Fargo processed $530 billion of debit card purchases across 10.5 billion transactions, according to its 2025 annual report, an average purchase value of just over $50. Based on those figures — which might overstate the covered activity by the bank — the current cap would translate to nearly $2.6 billion of fee revenue. The Fed's 2023 proposal would drop that to less than $1.9 billion. A base cap of 1 cent, keeping the current ad valorem and fraud adjustment rates, would drop it to around $470 million, a reduction of more than 80%.

"The debit economics of the large debit issuers will be destroyed, effectively," Grover said. "The largest issuers are not going to be able to sustain fee free accounts for consumers that have more modest relationships with them. The notion of free checking with all that entails could go away. We'll also see the delta between the covered programs and the exempt programs hugely magnified."

'No easy way out'

Interchange oversight was not a responsibility the Fed sought. It did not request it during the drafting of Dodd-Frank or the Durbin Amendment. But, it was assigned it all the same, with lawmakers noting that the Fed's expertise as an operator of its own payments system. Yet, whether or not the Fed wanted the authority, it isn't going away. 

In other recent cases, such as the banking industry lawsuit over stress testing, the Fed has been willing to accept the changing jurisprudence and opt for reform over litigation. But the matter of interchange is different. Not only does it bring into question the Fed's discretion, it also positions it between two formidable interest groups — banks and retailers — who are unlikely to settle for détente. 

"The Fed is between a rock and a hard place. The banks are on one side and they do not like the Durbin Amendment, the merchants are on the other side and they love it. Those are two well represented groups and there's no appeasing one without upsetting the other," Alvarez said. "The Fed has to do what it thinks is right, as it always does, but it's not going to lean for or against the banks for any reasons nor is it going to lean for or against the merchants for any reason. There is no easy way out of this one."

data.title: The Binance hack is a $6 billion warning shot to security chiefs
data.description:
I just got done reading Binance's initial report on its $6 billion hack, and it is eye opening. This was about as far from a Dillinger-style cash grab as you can get. The degree of planning and sophistication deployed makes the Oceans 11 crew look like they were knocking over a lemonade stand.

There will be a lot to chew on over this report. Already there are questions about the ethics of freezing digital assets, and whether banks should have any part in recovering the funds. But the most eye opening part of the whole report, to me at least, is the realization that as we move further and further into a completely digital financial system, this is going to become the norm. Defending against this exact kind of scheme is going to be table stakes in the future, which must be kept in mind as we move into a more digitized financial system.

The attack itself unfolded over about four hours on Oct. 29 online thieves drained about $6.34 billion worth of digital assets from wallets operated by Binance, which is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. They gained access to wallets that held bitcoin, XRP, ether and several other cryptos. The large transfers tripped a wire in Binance's internal systems and sent an alert, but it took the company several hours to completely block the pathways that gave the attackers access. But that four-hour period is only the end of the attack. The whole scheme began back in June.

In June, a Binance employee downloaded malware purporting to be an AI coding tool called Homebrew. The security team saw this and swapped the computer, but the downloaded malware still gave the attackers — widely believed to be state actors in North Korea — a look inside Binance's wallet network. In September, the malefactors went through a jobs website and contacted a different Binance engineer, pretending that they were recruiting him for a legitimate job.

They created a fake company with a fake CEO, a fake HR department and a fake HR representative with fake social media accounts. They conducted multiple interviews with the engineer. The HR rep shared their social media accounts. The CEO interviewed the engineer. They then asked the engineer to download a fake assignment, purportedly a test of their skills. 

The assignment was of course more malware, that not only installed itself within Binance's system, but hid its own tracks within the system. On Oct. 20, the attackers used an internal AI agent they'd gained access to to take over wallets overseen by two other Binance employees. On Oct. 29, they launched the attack.

This is not only the biggest robbery in the history of crypto markets, it may be the biggest robbery anywhere, ever. The largest bank robbery ever occurred in 2003, when Saddam Hussein sent his son to the Central Bank of Iraq with a handwritten note ordering the withdrawal of $1 billion. In 1972, seven men robbed $30 million from a branch of United California Bank. In 1988, a sophisticated group of robbers stole $640 million in bearer bonds from the vault of the Nakatomi Corp. in Los Angeles.

Okay, that last one is obviously just the plot of Die Hard. But you get my point. $6 billion is an incredible amount of money. And the thieves targeted Binance for a few reasons. Unlike physical money, digital money can be moved in huge amounts in virtually no time at all, transferred and transferred over and over, from wallet to wallet and through "tumblers" that mixed the digits so they are virtually untraceable. Indeed, while Binance froze about half of the stolen funds, the rest are almost certainly gone for good. Binance is reimbursing its customers from its own reserves.

More importantly: how secure is crypto? "Money" isn't a thing so much as a concept, and the laws and regulations that circumscribe how banks operate essentially defines what money is and how it is used. Those laws may feel like an endless burden, but they protect the money and that level of security is what makes people trust banks. 

Read more:

  • Forget jobs or inflation, credit is what matters. And credit is…
  • For both de novos and prediction markets, it's how you read the law
  • Those sleepy deposits that are 90% of your customers are waking up
  • Crypto and bitcoin have problems the CFTC and SEC can't fix

Only crypto degens leave their money on a platform like Binance. But as digital assets integrate into the traditional financial system, and normal people start using them, the most important part of that transition is going to be to port the security of the analog systems onto the digital systems. 

But as the Binance theft shows, protecting the money is going to involve a lot more than just filling out SARs reports, and this is something banks and banking regulators need to start hashing out now. In the regulated financial world, moving fast and breaking things is not an option.

data.title: Edward Jones CEO on the $1.4B Class B share sale and her succession plans
data.description:
• What's at stake: Edward Jones aims to raise $1.4 billion by selling a new class of ownership shares to fund its next phase, as its top leader plans her own succession. 
  • Key quote: "Five years from now, I won't be the right leader for this organization. And we will have the right person in place who will be." — Penny Pennington, CEO and managing partner of Edward Jones 

Edward Jones advisors are taking on a new type of ownership stake in the firm at roughly the pace expected, though some are waiting to see how it plays out.

That's how Managing Partner and CEO Penny Pennington characterized advisors' willingness to exchange their existing Edward Jones ownership stakes — known as Class A shares — for new Class B shares with payouts tied more directly to firm profits. The offer comes amid Edward Jones' plans to raise $1.4 billion through sales of the new Class B shares to employees.

Edward Jones remains one of the few wealth managers structured as employee-owned private partnerships. With more than 20,000 advisors and roughly $2.6 trillion in client assets, it is certainly the largest.

Pennington said in an interview Tuesday that the goal of the latest capital raise is to put ownership stakes in the hands of 35,000 of her roughly 55,000 colleagues. She declined to specify how many employees have already bought new Class B shares or elected to swap their Class A shares.

"But they're tracking right along with what we expected," Pennington said. "And the acceptance of our partnership capital is tracking right along with historic numbers, which is very high."

Edward Jones' current capital raise is the largest in its 100-year-plus history and its first since 2021. To arrive at $1.4 billion, Edward Jones aims to sell 1.4 million of the new Class B shares for $1,000 apiece. The minimum purchase allowed is $5,000.

Edward Jones employees who swap their Class A shares for Class B will be giving up a guaranteed payout of 7.5% on their capital contributions. The payments on Class B shares will instead be tied to firm profits and could go even higher.

Pennington said some partners likely want to see more of a track record with the Class B shares before making the swap.

"You know, let's see this work out for a year," Pennington said.

Pennington, managing partner of Edward Jones since 2019, sat down with Financial Planning this week at the firm's annual Innovation Summit near its hometown of St. Louis to discuss the reasons behind the switch to Class B shares, what Edward Jones plans to do with its capital raise and her own succession plans for the firm's top role.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length. 

Financial Planning: Why did Edward Jones offer the switch to Class B shares?

Penny Pennington: It really did three things. One, it opened the partnership to even more people. We've established the largest offering that we've ever done, the [$1.4 billion] that we're about to do. Now we plan to have an offering every couple of years. In the past, it had been every four years.

We also shifted some governance. So the managing partner has always had, along with our general partners, a 65-and-out clause. You have to be out at the end of the year that you turn 65. [Founder] Ted Jones put that in place. It just refreshes the partnership.

We've also established a 10-year term for the managing partner. I'll serve 10 years if my health holds.

We also established a vote by our general partners if there were to ever be a significant transaction, such as a proposed sale or dissolution of the partnership. And I've been very, very clear with our entire company a number of times: This partnership has never been for sale, and it will never be for sale. 

So what we did with the partnership amendment was to do everything possible to make sure that all of our colleagues know that this partnership is enduring into multiple generations. 

FP: Why the new payout system for Class B shares?

PP: To get real specific about that, the Class A partnership — there was only one class of limited partnership in the past — had that provision for a 7.5% guaranteed rate. That was an interest expense, actually, on our operating statement. 

Then the remainder of return that goes to the LPs [limited partners] then came out of net income. We're switching that to Class B. 

What it helps us do, frankly, is to ensure that our partnership capital looks more like partnership capital rather than part of the return looking like an interest expense. 

FP: Is there an accounting reason for this?

PP: Not exactly an accounting reason. It's because the interest expense comes out above our bonus profit line, and it was actually sub-optimizing the level of bonus for our colleagues. So if we take that interest expense line out, and just have it be part of LP returns after everything is at the bottom line, then we don't sub-optimize the bonus any longer. 

FP: Why would partners trade their Class A shares for Class B?

PP: Because anything that we've ever done for the partnership improves the situation for the partner. So from the standpoint of why we did this, it's strengthening the partnership without diminishing the rate of return for the LPs. In fact, in some cases, Class B could actually be a little bit higher than Class A. 

FP: The capital you've raised in recent years has been used to pay for some pretty big changes at Edward Jones. Where is the firm generally headed?

PP: So what we've been changing over the years is really moving Edward Jones from one good way of serving everybody, to more tailored, hyper-personalized, relevant ways for them across the arc of their lives, across wealth bands. 

What that's meant for us is that we've segmented our business. So our core clients generally have $250,000 to $3 million in assets. Now our new-to-wealth clients — those who are just getting started — will go at the beginning of next year to a digital platform with advice built in and a hybrid advisor in the background. This is brand new for Edward Jones. That's going to attract those who are more digitally forward with slightly less complex needs. 

And then on the other end, we have Edward Jones Generations and Private Wealth. We're winning business there. They were business owners, ranchers, farmers, corporate executives. We can marshal their resources to grow into high net worth clients. Now we have the advice, the capabilities, the products to help them. 

Options will be coming out at the beginning of next year. We're already in alternatives, structured notes and IPOs. That's a different Edward Jones than it has been in the past. But the ethos underlying it remains the same. We want to help more people improve their lives and achieve their financial fulfillment. 

FP: Are there business reasons that make working with clients with $250,000 to $3 million in assets difficult? How can technology help?

PP: You know, we have always invested in this hyperlocal business model — that some would say is actually very expensive — where we put up branches all over the country in order to be where people are. Some could say that's a sunk cost, quote unquote, in all that brick and mortar. 

Now you combine that with great technology that can enable the capacity to serve more people more completely according to their needs. Then you enable a digitally forward model. Our branch teams may not be giving the very best service to some of those lower-asset clients, and a digital forward experience can actually be an even better experience for them right now. 

FP: Where does AI come in?

PP: I like to focus on AI in three dimensions. Automation. So, take a business process that a human being doesn't want to do anyway because it's drudgery and automate it.

Then there's augmentation. The best example is a financial advisor whose insights and judgment can be augmented by having at their fingertips insights that come from 100,000 client conversations a day. That can be dynamically imparted to them as they're thinking about, "I've got a new client coming in, a single mom. She's got a special-needs child. She's got parents that she might be worried about caregiving for in the future. She's worried about her retirement plan, and her business is in growth mode. How do I really help this client?"

That may be an N-of-1 for that practice, but we've seen that client a couple thousand times a day. So how can we augment that financial advisor's discovery process?

Then there is addition. The example that I use most often is that 10 years ago, without the compute power that we have today, you simply could not dynamically rebalance a $100,000 portfolio in a tax-efficient way. But because of the algorithms that we have built vis-a-vis our investment model and the investment tools that we have available, our purchase of the Natixis tax overlay last year, we can dynamically rebalance a $100,000 portfolio just as easily as we can a $100 million portfolio.

FP: You also recently secured regulatory approval to have an industrial bank. How will that help the firm and its clients?

PP: Edward Jones Bank will open in January. The insight there, of course, is that clients, investors, the cognitive load of trying to put together their entire financial and life plan — it's just too much.
