They want things simplified, and so that's the insight around the Edward Jones Bank. 

We still have a partnership with U.S. Bank for checking accounts. The Edward Jones Bank will move us into lending, and then Edward Jones and our financial advisors will put all of that together for our clients. It'll be more digitally forward than it's ever been.

FP: What are your thoughts about advisor recruiting in the industry? Are the recruiting deals becoming too generous, and is Edward Jones placing a greater emphasis on recruiting?

PP: Our general approach is taking responsibility for growing the access to human advice. So there are 280,000 licensed producers today. There were 310,000 or 320,000 just a few years ago, and 100,000 of them are going to be gone over the next 10 or 15 years because of retirement. 

So Edward Jones really takes responsibility in this, and we will continue to hire financial advisors into different tracks. We'll hire financial advisors into teams for their career. We'll also hire financial advisors into teams with an apprentice approach, where they learn the nature of that practice and determine if they might stay in that practice or if they might become a practitioner themselves and build their own team. 

I also want to be very clear that we will continue to hire people into sole practitioner practices where it makes sense for them, for that marketplace, for the network that they have, and the practice that they want to build. 

So we're going to continue to build at the rate of 1% to 3% a year, in terms of the number of financial advisors that we're hiring. 

Now we hire some financial advisors from the industry. It's not the lion's share of whom we hire, and we're always looking for folks who understand a client-led strategy for serving clients through the nature of our culture and our private partnership. 

Our recruiting packages are very competitive. And when you get here, the approach at Edward Jones is more partner-like, I believe, than it is at many other firms. That's one of the things that really attracts people. 

FP: You mentioned earlier on that managing partners are now on a 10-year timeline before they have to leave and make room for someone else. How far along are you, and have you started planning for the succession?

PP: I came into this role on Jan. 1, 2019. The first notes that I took on my succession were in February of 2019. So I've been working on succession for eight years. 

This is what good leadership does, right? It's constantly thinking about developing the next generation of leaders and ensuring that every leadership team is stocked with people with unique perspectives, with unique backgrounds. It's why my executive leadership team, my enterprise leadership team, has completely turned over since I became managing partner. And a third of the team has been with our firm less than five years.

In many ways, I was an unlikely CEO. I was likely in the respect that I had been a financial advisor with Edward Jones and all of our managing partners had been a financial advisor with Edward Jones, building a practice in one way or another. But I was a transplant into this industry 14 years into my career. Yeah, I am the first managing partner who never knew Ted Jones, so this was a generational transference. 

So I was unlikely in some ways. But I like to think that I've been the right leader to match the moment. But five years from now, I won't be the right leader for this organization. And we will have the right person in place who will be.

data.title: Chainalysis discloses apparent breach of customers' accounts
data.description:
• Key insight: Chainalysis said Wednesday night that some customers' accounts appear to have been accessed without authorization and that password hashes and live tokens for all of its users got exposed to an attacker, five days after saying it had found no evidence of access to credentials or session tokens.
  • What's at stake: Banks and crypto companies use the company's monitoring service to check whether money is tied to theft, sanctions or laundering, and Chainalysis' status page still listed it as "Under Maintenance" Thursday afternoon.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

Chainalysis, which sells tools to banks for screening crypto transactions, disclosed late Wednesday that an intruder appears to have gotten into some of its customers' accounts in what seems as of Thursday afternoon to be a live cybersecurity incident.

Chainalysis is notifying customers whose accounts on KYT (short for Know Your Transaction), its transaction-monitoring tool, "appear to have been accessed without authorization," according to the company's post on the incident, which it first published Oct. 30 and has updated several times since.

Banks and crypto companies use tools such as KYT to check whether money moving through their platforms is tied to theft, sanctions or money laundering. They use KYT to view risk scores and alerts, set alert thresholds and upload lists of crypto addresses to monitor, according to its product page.

The company has not said how much of that information an intruder could see or change or how long any intruder had access.

Chainalysis also has not said whether it has removed the intruder from its systems. A customer email Chainalysis quoted in its Wednesday morning update called the incident "an ongoing multifront cyberattack" and said one method of attack had been "contained and remediated."

Chainalysis said in the post that, at this time, it has "no evidence that any investigation data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." Attribution data links crypto addresses to the people and companies behind them.

Password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users also got exposed to an attacker, according to the post.

A password hash is a scrambled version of a password. Tokens generally let a person or program act as a logged-in user without re-entering a password, but the post does not specify what an intruder could see or change using a live token.

Chainalysis made these disclosures five days after it said in the post that it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens."

Awkward timing

Chainalysis took KYT offline Wednesday and intended to begin restoring access Thursday, according to the post. The company's status page still listed KYT as "Under Maintenance" as of 4 p.m. Eastern that day.

The shutdown came as the crypto industry tries to stop thieves from cashing out what they took from Binance, though the first version of Chainalysis' post said the incident is not related to that theft.

Thieves stole $6.4 billion from the crypto exchange six days before KYT went offline, and about $3.35 billion still sat in addresses linked to the theft as of early Thursday, according to a post from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.

Only a "negligible amount" has likely been cashed out, according to the Elliptic post. The thieves need "a counterparty, such as a centralized exchange," to turn the funds into money they can spend, and that is where "the funds can be identified and stopped," the post said.

KYT is sold for that job. "Top crypto exchanges rely on Chainalysis," according to the KYT product page, which says the tool helps customers trace illicit funds and prepare to take action "such as freezing funds."

What Chainalysis said, and when

Chainalysis first publicly disclosed the incident Oct. 30, posting a customer email that said an outside actor used "offensive agentic techniques" to break into its systems.

The email did not define the phrase. "Agentic" typically refers to AI software that can carry out multi-step tasks on its own, suggesting the attacker used such software in the break-in. The email cited "an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks" but did not specify that AI drove this one.

The attacker accessed customer data such as user IDs, full names, email addresses and labels for users' roles, according to the email.

On Monday, Chainalysis said in an update that it had taken its Reactor investigations tool and a product called Data Solutions offline.

Reactor lets investigators trace crypto funds and identify who is behind transactions, and Data Solutions delivers Chainalysis' blockchain data directly to customers' own systems, according to the company's website.

The company kept compliance products running because of "their role in detecting money laundering across the ecosystem," the update said. Those products included KYT, according to the company's status page.

Wednesday morning, the company issued an update on the post, saying an "on-path attack" (in which an intruder gets between two systems and reads their traffic) exposed "a subset of customer passwords."

Less than an hour later, in another update, Chainalysis said it had taken KYT offline because of "abnormal activity."

"On Monday, we discovered certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor," the company said in an update Wednesday night. The company's Monday update had not mentioned passwords or tokens.

The post does not say how the "subset of customer passwords" exposed in the on-path attack relates to the password hashes exposed for all users.

A Chainalysis spokesperson did not say how many KYT accounts were accessed or when customers learned of the token exposure.

"We are not sharing additional information beyond what has been published in the blog," the spokesperson told American Banker.

Banks Chainalysis has named as customers

Chainalysis claims more than 1,500 customers in 70 countries, according to its webpage for financial institutions. That count is not limited to banks, and the spokesperson did not say how many banks or credit unions use the company's products.

BNY "integrated the full Chainalysis compliance suite into its risk management program," according to the same webpage. A 2022 Chainalysis post said that suite included KYT and Reactor.

A September 2025 Chainalysis post said Lead Bank implemented Reactor and VASP Risking, a tool for rating the risk of crypto businesses. Reactor has been offline since Monday.

Nothing Chainalysis has published says whether any bank's account was accessed. Spokespeople for BNY and Lead Bank did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Getting back online

To regain access to KYT and Address Screening (a related product), customers must give Chainalysis trusted IP addresses, which identify the networks from which they connect, according to the Wednesday night update.

Users must then reset passwords and replace their API keys, which are the credentials software uses to connect to the service.

The update gave no date for the return of Reactor and Data Solutions, and it did not say how customers should screen transactions in the meantime.

data.title: Fintech targets small-business niche that banks have spurned
data.description:
• Key takeaway: LoanBud is looking for partners, including banks and credit unions, to participate in a new platform that links the buyers and sellers of small businesses with modest price tags. It's a market that traditional lenders have typically shied away from.
  • Expert quote: "If you factor in the experience and capital access of the borrower, I think it becomes more interesting." — Legacy Entrepreneurs CEO Joseph Steigman

Burke Purcell began his financial-services career helping self-employed entrepreneurs obtain mortgages. He created LoanBud, a fintech marketplace that links qualified borrowers with Small Business Administration lenders, after multiple entreaties from mortgage clients who needed assistance finding business loans.

Now, Purcell believes he's found a promising new niche — one that is almost totally overlooked by banks and credit unions.

In October, the privately held LoanBud launched a new marketplace, LoanBud Acquire, to finance small-business acquisitions with sales prices between $100,000 and $350,000. The marketplace operates outside the SBA loan market, focusing on established small businesses where a prequalified buyer is willing to contribute a 15% equity-capital injection.

LoanBud Acquire is currently working with a select group of capital providers, but Purcell said growing demand for the program is creating opportunities for additional partners, including banks and credit unions.

"We would love participation in this program," Purcell told American Banker. "The more liquidity that wants to get into this space, the stronger we are."

But adding partners may be easier said than done. While LoanBud's SBA marketplace counts more than 50 bank capital partners, virtually none have shown interest in making small-dollar acquisition loans at scale, according to Purcell. 

"They just don't have the desire for it," Purcell said. 

Historically, lenders have sidestepped small-dollar business acquisitions since it takes just as long to underwrite them as deals with higher price tags. They've also expressed concern about small firms' capacity to handle the debt they'd need to incur. The lack of a loan guarantee from the SBA is an additional deterrent.

As a result, small-dollar acquisitions are financed mostly through buyer capital, seller financing or some combination of the two, according to Purcell, who is LoanBud's founder and CEO.

"There's really not a great way for a lot of these smaller, owner-operated, real Main Street businesses to be able to get financed," Purcell said. 

Joseph Steigman, the founder of a Nashville, Tennessee-based brokerage that helps owners sell their small businesses, echoed Purcell. Steigman said he often has difficulty interesting banks in smaller deals.

"The ones that are willing to do them are hard to find," Steigman told American Banker.  

Steigman said he is "sympathetic to the amount of effort" involved in underwriting a loan, but he added that lenders who eschew smaller transactions are often passing up solid, bankable customers.

"If you factor in the experience and capital access of the borrower, I think it becomes more interesting," said Steigman, the founder of Legacy Entrepreneurs. 

"If the new owner has access to some of their own capital or sources of income, and the business is fundamentally sound with a good growth thesis around it … then leveraging the deal a little bit can make everybody happy."

Steigman, who has used LoanBud, said a technology platform like the one LoanBud has built can be successful at mapping out a small-acquisition borrower's experience and finances.

"You can kind of bucket that out and say, this person has all these experience indicators that are good, and also in their personal finances they've exited a business before and have cash reserves," Steigman said.

LoanBud, founded in 2022, recently closed its inaugural acquisition loan: a $350,000 loan to finance the sale of a sushi restaurant in Texas. Purcell said he hopes it's the first of many, bringing change to what he termed a "massively underserved market."

"A $250,000 acquisition matters just as much to the buyer, the seller and the employees as a multimillion-dollar transaction," Purcell said.

data.title: Black banks' merger stays on track despite push to derail it
data.description:
• Key insight: Two Black-owned banks in the Carolinas expect their proposed merger to be approved by the end of the year, after fending off another bid this fall.
  • What's at stake: The deal, which still needs regulatory approval, would create the largest Black-owned bank in the nation, based on total asset size, while also reducing the number of Black-owned banks in the U.S. to 16.

The proposed merger of two Black-owned banks in the Southeast is closer to being finalized after a vote by shareholders of the selling company served to rebuff a third bank's effort to derail the deal.

M&F Bancorp in Durham, North Carolina, and Optus Financial in Columbia, South Carolina, now await regulatory approval for the $105 million transaction, in which M&F is set to be acquired by Optus to create the largest Black-owned banks in the country. If it closes, the acquisition would reduce the number of Black-owned banks in the U.S. to 16.

In a press release, the banks said they continue to expect the all-cash deal to close by the end of this year.

The shareholder vote came during a contentious period in which another suitor, Triad Business Bank in Greensboro, North Carolina, argued that M&F's plan to be acquired by Optus would be a bad deal for its shareholders.

Triad also maintained that the Optus deal would be a negative development for Black-owned banks, whose existence has dwindled amid struggles to obtain capital, invest in operations and compete with non-Black-owned banks.

The preliminary results from a Wednesday vote by M&F's shareholders show that nearly 74% of the shares entitled to vote on the deal voted in favor of it, M&F said. The vote was initially scheduled to take place on Oct. 7, but it was adjourned until Oct. 20 and then adjourned again until Wednesday. M&F had previously indicated that the delays were meant to give M&F shareholders enough time to consider a counter-proposal by Triad.

James Sills III, M&F's president and CEO, said in a statement Wednesday that the results mark "an important milestone" for the $503.5 million-asset bank, which was founded in 1907.

The combination of Optus and M&F, which will have roughly $1.3 billion of assets, will be "positioned to expand access to capital and economic opportunity across the Carolinas," Sills added.

Liberty Bank & Trust in New Orleans, Louisiana, is currently the largest Black-owned bank, with $1.1 billion of assets as of June 30, according to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.

Optus and M&F must still receive approval or non-objections from four regulators: the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the North Carolina Commissioner of Banks and the South Carolina Board of Financial Institutions, according to M&F's disclosures. The banks have filed applications with each regulator, M&F has said.

Triad responded Thursday to the shareholder vote with a statement saying it is "grateful to the shareholders, employees and customers who listened and considered our proposals to create a better outcome for them, for Parrish Street and for North Carolina." Parrish Street, where M&F was founded, is a commercial district in Durham that was once known as "Black Wall Street." 

"We respect their decision," Triad added.

The $536 million-asset Triad, which is not Black-owned, published a detailed report last week arguing that its most recent proposal was superior to the one M&F accepted from Optus in July. 

Triad's plan called for preserving M&F's name, charter and status as a minority depository institution. It also called for writing into the charter that the bank's board must be majority African-American, and it emphasized the fact that the 119-year-old M&F will cease to exist if it's sold to Optus.

Triad has criticized M&F for not lending more of its capital, and for awarding bonuses worth a combined $2.6 million to the board and management earlier this year.

Part of Triad's argument was that M&F's shareholders would get a better deal from Triad, even though Triad's offer would leave them with a bit less than half of the shares of the combined company. Triad projected that the combined bank's tangible book value per share would rise from $29.87 at the deal's closing to between $44.52 and $49.50 five years later.

Terms of the Optus deal call for shareholders to receive up to $53.30 per share of common stock, payable in cash, starting with a cash payment of $46.57. An additional cash payment of $6.73 could be payable at a later date, depending on whether M&F successfully redeems certain preferred stock prior to or within 12 months of the acquisition.

In Wednesday's press release, M&F noted that shareholder approval of the Optus deal came amid "unsolicited proposals" from Triad. It said its board, with help from financial and legal advisors, "considered those proposals and continued to recommend the Optus transaction." M&F also said it did not "intend to comment further" on the Triad proposals.

Under the terms of the Optus acquisition, Sills will become CEO of Optus Financial and Optus Bank. Paul Mitchell, chairman of Optus Financial and its bank subsidiary, will continue in his current role. 

Read more:

  • Democrats sweep Congress, setting up years of oversight for banks
  • $6.4 billion Binance heist leaves banks off the hook
  • Lenders paint bleak picture of consumer credit in 3Q survey
  • Key Senate Democrat vows probe into banks linked to Epstein

The two merging banks have not said if Benita Lefft, president of Optus Bank, will have a role with the combined company post-acquisition. 

Two years ago, Lefft succeeded Dominik Mjartan, who had been president and CEO since 2017 and led the bank through a period of enormous growth and profitability. Optus, which was founded in 1999, had about $764 million of assets as of June 30, according to the FDIC.

Post-acquisition, Optus is set to operate 10 branches, including eight in North Carolina that are currently operated by M&F.

data.title: Chime puts out the welcome mat for external AI agents
data.description:
• Key insights: Chime will allow its customers to bring their own AI into its ecosystem, and work in tandem with its own AI assistant, Jade. 
  • What's at stake: Financial institutions have been split on whether to allow external AI agents into their digital systems. 

As financial institutions decide whether to allow external AI agents into their digital ecosystems, Chime is preparing to enable customers to both bring their own agent and engage with Chime's in-house agent, Jade. 

Chime is building secure connections to general-purpose AI agents, which will allow Chime members to use their preferred agent while staying in control of who can access their accounts and what actions agents can take with their money, CEO Chris Britt said on the company's third-quarter earnings call. 

Those agents will work in tandem with Jade, Chime's personal AI assistant that provides financial coaching and spending insights. 

"We don't believe that a single agent will be best suited to manage every area of your life. Researching a major purchase or planning a trip is one thing. In more complex, regulated categories like healthcare and finance, we believe that trusted specialist agents will win," Britt said. 

"When asking an agent to move money, pay bills, or manage investments, you need more than intelligence. You need financial expertise, safeguards you can trust, and accountability for every action. And that's why our biggest bet is Jade, our personal finance agent for Chime members and ultimately all consumers," Britt said. 

Chime's product development can also benefit from the AI boom, Britt said, noting that AI agents will make it easier for "consumers to find better-value financial products and switch institutions, eroding the inertia that has protected big banks for decades."

AI was one of four key growth areas, including Chime Prime, its lending businesses and its pending acquisition of Stride Bank, that Chime said was key to its continued growth and the expansion of its total addressable market to consumers that make up to $200,000 in annual salary. 

Revenue for the third quarter ended September 30 grew 32% from the prior year to $718 million, up from a 27% growth rate last quarter and 25% growth rate in the first quarter. Net income was $43.7 million, marking the company's third quarter of profitability and ahead of analysts estimates of $38.2 million, according to S&P CapitalIQ. In the third quarter of last year, Chime posted a $54.7 million loss. 

Purchase volume increased 19% compared to the prior year to $38.5 billion, and 22% to $40 billion when including outbound instant transfers. And active members increased 20% year over year to 10.9 million, with 500,000 new customers added since the second quarter and approximately 1.8 million members over the last year. 

Average revenue per active member, one of Chime's most important key performance indicators, increased 10% from the prior year to $270. Notably, members that are part of Chime premium membership tier called Chime Prime, have double the average revenue per active member compared to non-Prime members, President and interim Chief Financial Officer Mark Troughton said during the call, noting that Chime was growing faster than the company anticipated. 

Chime also said its lifetime-value-to-customer-acquisition-cost ratio, which the company uses to evaluate the success of its massive marketing budget, was nearly 10x, up from about 8x when the company went public. 

"Chime sits in the digital banking sweet spot… having cracked the code on new member acquisition at compelling 10x LTV/CAC unit economics with strong interchange and short-term liquidity monetization," Andrew Jeffrey, an analyst at William Blair, said in a research note.  "Accelerating [monthly active user] growth, better [average revenue per active member], stable credit quality, a strong product pipeline, and ample operating leverage are a potent recipe for multiple expansion."

Momentum in Chime Prime and the company's lending businesses — which include its earned wage access product MyPay, its overdraft protection product SpotMe and its short duration installment loans called Instant Loans — and growth in Chime Prime helped underscore strong results for the quarter, according to Keefe Bruyette and Woods analyst Sanjay Sakhrani. 

Originations across its three lending products hit $50 billion in annualized volume, with an average duration of two weeks and a loss ready around 1%. MyPay originations hit $5.3 billion, generating more than $500 million in annualized revenue during the quarter, Britt said. Chime doubled the maximum MyPay limit to $1,000 during the quarter. 

Instant Loans grew at a faster rate, with origination volume during the quarter growing to $381 million. More than 20% of active members use the product, Britt said. 

"Our lending products deepen our primary account relationships, and they're becoming a bigger driver of RPAM and transaction profit," Britt said. "We're now taking the same disciplined playbook to new products, including our unsecured line of credit currently in beta, and an unsecured credit card in employee testing that we expect to roll out next year." 

Chime's acquisition of Stride Bank is also expected to be an approximately $100 billion windfall for the payments fintech that will lower the company's cost of funds, Troughton said. The bank charter will also allow Chime to offer its lending products in all 50 states and stop paying sponsor bank fees. 

Chime would have had about $6.5 billion in total assets, which includes about $1.6 billion in commercial loans, as of the end of September across both its banking partners. The company also reiterated that Chime intends to stay asset light and below the $10 billion threshold for the "foreseeable future," and that if it were to cross that threshold, it would be "because the economic benefits of crossing it are greater than the costs of crossing it," Troughton said. 

"If we ever do get close to that level — and we hope we will — there are active capital markets for us," Troughton said. "Our assets here are very attractive. They're short duration, they're low risk, underwritten by direct deposit with unique underwriting signals.There's a very active market for us to be able to get some assistance with those assets."
